concepts.title: Habits
concepts.hook: Missing one day did not undo a new habit in Lally's 12-week study. Habits were estimated to take from 18 to 254 days to settle in.
concepts.rule: A cue can start a learned act. Repeating it in the same place makes the link stronger. In Lally's study, habits took very different times to settle, and one missed day did not undo them.

claims.text: Cues in a stable setting, like a place or an act just before, can bring back a learned action with little thought.
In Lally's 84-day study, the estimated time to near full habit strength ranged from 18 to 254 days, and one missed chance did not undo habit growth.
In that study, the middle estimated time to near full habit strength was 66 days, among the 39 people whose data fit the curve well.
Early repeats in the same setting add the most to how automatic an act feels; later repeats add less and less.
Students who moved to a new university kept old habits mainly when parts of the old setting stayed the same.
Lally's team notes that in an earlier study, missing a whole week, unlike one day, made later practice less likely.

items.stem: Kunal opens his flashcard app each time his train pulls out of Dadar. This week he takes a bus instead. What is most likely?

options.text: He opens it as usual, since he still wants to revise.
options.feedback: Wanting to revise is not the same as the cue. Without the train, the act is less likely.

options.text: He forgets the app more often.
options.feedback: With the train gone, the cue is gone too, so the app is easier to forget.

options.text: He opens it more, to make up for it.
options.feedback: A missing cue makes the act less likely, not more.

items.stem: Ishaan thinks pure willpower drives his evening sit-ups. Yet he does them only right after the TV goes off. Why does that point to a cue?

options.text: Willpower is strongest just after watching TV.
options.feedback: Nothing shows willpower peaks then. The fixed moment is the sign of a cue.

options.text: Sit-ups count for more when the TV is off.
options.feedback: The TV going off does not change the sit-ups. It is the signal that starts them.

options.text: The act follows the same moment each time.
options.feedback: When an act always comes right after one moment, that moment is working as a cue.

items.stem: Put the growth of Rehan's after-dinner guitar habit in order.

options.text: Dinner ends, and that becomes his cue to play.
options.feedback: The cue comes first: the end of dinner starts the act.

options.text: The first weeks of playing bring big gains in ease.
options.feedback: Early repeats in the same setting add the most.

options.text: Later weeks add smaller and smaller gains.
options.feedback: As the curve nears its plateau, each repeat adds less.

options.text: Playing after dinner now needs little thought.
options.feedback: Near the plateau, the cue starts the act almost by itself.

items.stem: In the hostel, Pia's new push-up habit still gets easier each day. Raj's push-ups barely change any more. Working back from that, whose habit is likely older?

options.text: Raj's, since gains level off later on.
options.feedback: Right. Early repeats bring big jumps and later ones add little, so a habit that barely changes is further along.

options.text: Pia's, since big daily gains mean a long run.
options.feedback: Big daily gains come early. A habit that still jumps each day is most likely the newer one.

options.text: Neither; gains look the same at any age.
options.feedback: Repeats add the most early and less later, so the size of the daily gain hints at a habit's age.

items.stem: In Lally's 12-week habit study, about what was the middle estimated time, in days, for an act to feel automatic?

options.text: About 66 days.
options.feedback: Right. The middle estimate was about 66 days, though single people ranged from 18 to 254.

options.text: About 30 days.
options.feedback: Thirty days is too short. The middle estimate in the study was about 66 days, over two months.

options.text: About 254 days.
options.feedback: That was the longest estimate, not the middle one. The middle was about 66 days.

items.stem: Missing one day did little harm to Neel's morning jog. Then exams make him skip a full week. Why could this gap matter more?

options.text: A habit resets to zero after any single miss, big or small.
options.feedback: One missed day did not undo habit growth, so a reset after any miss is wrong.

options.text: A week of missed chances can hold a habit back.
options.feedback: One miss did little harm in the study, but a whole week off made later practice less likely in earlier work.

options.text: Exams make every habit stronger.
options.feedback: Nothing here says exams help habits. The long gap is the problem.

misconceptions.name: One fixed day count
misconceptions.correction: Habit time varies by person and act; there is no fixed day count.

misconceptions.name: One miss resets all
misconceptions.correction: One missed chance did not wipe out habit growth in the study.

misconceptions.name: Goal replaces cue
misconceptions.correction: A steady goal may not start a habit when a usual cue is gone.

misconceptions.name: Every repeat adds the same
misconceptions.correction: Early repeats add the most; later repeats add less and less.

steps.title: A cue starts a habit

hook.stem: Why do many people grab their phone the moment they get home?

options.text: Getting home sets it off.
options.feedback: Right. Walking in the door is the cue, so the phone comes out with little thought.

options.text: They decide to, every single time.
options.feedback: A habit needs little deciding. The cue of getting home starts it.

options.text: Phones send more alerts in the evening.
options.feedback: Alerts can play a part, but the habit is set off by getting home.

steps.teach: A habit often starts with a cue: a place, a time or an act just before it. The cue sets the act off, so you barely decide.

parts: After brushing his teeth,
Arun does ten push-ups.
example.spot: After brushing his teeth,
example.feedback: Brushing his teeth comes first each time, so it is the cue for the push-ups.

guided.stem: Ravi studies well at the library desk, but not at home. What might be missing at home?
guided.hint: Which thing is only in one place?

options.text: The desk cue.
options.feedback: Right. The library desk is a cue that his home does not have.

options.text: His wish to study.
options.feedback: He wants to study in both places. The setting is what differs.

options.text: His books.
options.feedback: He can carry his books home. The library desk stays behind.

steps.takeaway: Find the cue, and you find what starts the habit.

steps.title: Early repeats count most

hook.stem: Week one of a new routine or week ten: when does each day of practice add more?

options.text: In week one.
options.feedback: Right. Early repeats bring the biggest jumps in how easy the act feels.

options.text: In week ten.
options.feedback: By week ten the gains are small. The big jumps come early.

options.text: Every week adds the same.
options.feedback: In one study the gains shrank over time, so the weeks were not equal.

steps.teach: Each repeat in the same setting makes the act more automatic. Early repeats add the most, and later ones add less, so the gains level off.

parts: In week one, Sana's morning walk goes from hard to fairly easy,
in week six it gets a little easier,
and by week ten it barely changes.
example.spot: In week one, Sana's morning walk goes from hard to fairly easy,
example.feedback: The first week brings the biggest change, because early repeats add the most.

guided.stem: Asha's rope routine now starts without effort. She wants a new stretching habit. Should she expect that one to begin fully automatic?
guided.hint: Ask where a brand-new act sits on the curve.

options.text: No, it needs its own early repeats.
options.feedback: Right. Each act climbs its own curve, so the stretching starts at the steep early part, not at the top.

options.text: Yes, her rope habit carries over to it.
options.feedback: Her rope routine got easy through its own repeats. A new act has had none yet, so it starts low.

options.text: Yes, once she has one habit, new ones start easy.
options.feedback: The curve is built by repeats of that act in its setting. A new act starts near the bottom.

steps.takeaway: Early repeats build a habit most; later ones add less.

steps.title: Weeks, not a fixed count, and one miss is fine

hook.stem: A poster says every habit takes exactly 21 days. Is that right?

options.text: No, it varies a lot.
options.feedback: Right. In one study the time ranged from a few weeks to many months.

options.text: Yes, 21 days for everyone.
options.feedback: No single count fits everyone. In one study times varied widely.

options.text: It takes about one week.
options.feedback: One week is too short for most people in the study.

steps.teach: In one 12-week study, habits were estimated to take 18 to 254 days to feel automatic, middle 66. One missed day did no harm, so a slip is fine, but a week off can set it back.

visual.label: Estimated days until a habit felt automatic, in one 12-week study

example.ask: Tap what happened after the miss.
parts: Meena missed her morning run once.
The next day, the run still felt automatic.
example.spot: The next day, the run still felt automatic.
example.feedback: One missed day did not wipe out weeks of practice, so her run stayed automatic.

guided.stem: Kiran has meditated daily for three weeks, but it still takes effort. What does this show?
guided.hint: Compare three weeks with the middle time in the study.

options.text: It can take a couple of months.
options.feedback: Right. In one study the middle time was about two months.

options.text: He is doing it wrong.
options.feedback: Effort at three weeks is normal. Many people need longer.

options.text: This habit is not going to form.
options.feedback: Three weeks is early. Many people take two months or more.

steps.takeaway: Give it weeks, and do not worry about one missed day.

concepts.title: Loss aversion
concepts.hook: In choice studies, people often act as if losing ₹100 counts for more than winning ₹100.
concepts.rule: Loss aversion is a pattern in choices: people act as if a loss counts for more than a same-size gain, about twice on average. It depends on the start point, and it is a tendency, not a law for every person.

claims.text: Gains and losses are judged from a reference point, which is often where you start or what you expected.
A loss tends to weigh more than a gain of the same size, so most people dislike a fair 50-50 bet, more so as the stake grows.
Across 607 estimates from 150 papers, a loss weighed about twice a gain of the same size, on average. The figures varied from study to study.

items.stem: Tanmay can swap his ₹500 match ticket for a friend's ticket to another match he would enjoy just as much. He refuses, in case the swap turns out worse. What is pulling on him?

options.text: A possible loss counts for more than the same gain.
options.feedback: Right. In choices, the chance of ending up worse counts for more than the chance of ending up better, so he refuses an even swap.

options.text: The new match is sure to be worse.
options.feedback: He would enjoy both just as much. What holds him back is how a possible loss feels, not the match.

options.text: A loss and a gain of one size count the same for him.
options.feedback: If they counted the same, an even swap would not bother him. In choices, a possible loss usually weighs more.

items.stem: Why do more people turn down a fair coin toss for ₹10,000 than one for ₹10?

options.text: Big stakes make the fifty-fifty odds unfair to the player.
options.feedback: The odds stay fifty-fifty. It is the size of the possible loss that changes.

options.text: Dislike of fair bets grows as the stake grows.
options.feedback: The pull of a possible loss gets stronger with a bigger stake, so more people say no.

options.text: People enjoy losing small sums.
options.feedback: Nobody needs to enjoy losing. A small loss simply weighs less than a big one.

items.stem: Ananya says her ₹400 pocket money this month feels like a cut. What was most likely true before?

options.text: She used to get less than ₹400.
options.feedback: Then ₹400 would feel like a rise, not a cut.

options.text: Prices in the shop went down.
options.feedback: Lower prices would make her money go further, not feel like a cut.

options.text: She used to get more than ₹400.
options.feedback: A result feels like a loss when it sits below the start, so her old amount was higher.

items.stem: A college fest has two notices: “Register early and save ₹100” and “Register late and pay ₹100 more.” The price gap is the same. Which notice likely pushes more students to sign up early?

options.text: The pay-more notice, which frames it as a loss.
options.feedback: The same ₹100 framed as a loss from the early price tends to weigh more than a saving.

options.text: The save notice, since saving feels best.
options.feedback: Savings are gains, and gains tend to weigh less than losses of the same size.

options.text: Neither, since the gap is the same.
options.feedback: The money gap is the same, but the start point in the wording changes how it feels.

items.stem: Pooled across many papers, about how many times as much as a same-size gain did a loss weigh, on average?

options.text: About 2 times.
options.feedback: Right. Pooled across studies, a loss weighed about twice a gain of the same size, on average.

options.text: About 1 time, the same.
options.feedback: If they weighed the same, people would take fair bets happily. On average a loss weighed about twice as much.

options.text: About 10 times.
options.feedback: That is far too high. The pooled average was about twice, though single studies differed.

items.stem: Your cousin hears that losses weigh twice as much, and says this holds for every person in every choice. Which reply fits best?

options.text: It holds for each person, since many studies agree.
options.feedback: Many studies were pooled, but their figures differed, so it is an average.

options.text: It is false, since some studies found less.
options.feedback: Some found less and some more. The average still came out near two.

options.text: It is an average across studies, and people vary.
options.feedback: Studies gave different figures, so twice is a middle value, not a fixed rule for each person.

misconceptions.name: Equal feel
misconceptions.correction: Equal gain and loss can have a different felt weight.

misconceptions.name: Always true
misconceptions.correction: The pattern does not fix how every person will feel.

misconceptions.name: Wording never matters
misconceptions.correction: The same result can feel like a gain or a loss, depending on the start point it is framed from.

steps.title: A loss feels bigger than a gain

hook.stem: A friend offers a coin toss: heads you win ₹100, tails you pay ₹100. Do most people take it?

options.text: No, most say no.
options.feedback: Right. Most people turn down a fair toss like this, because the loss weighs more.

options.text: Yes, since it is fair.
options.feedback: It is fair on paper, but most people still say no to it.

options.text: Just the people who dislike games say no.
options.feedback: It is not about liking games. Most people turn it down.

steps.teach: In choices, a loss usually counts for more than a gain of the same size. That is why most people turn down a fair coin toss for money, and more say no as the stake grows.

example.ask: Tap the choice the loss shaped.
parts: Sahil is offered a coin toss: win ₹50 or lose ₹50,
and though the odds are even, he says no.
example.spot: and though the odds are even, he says no.
example.feedback: The odds are even, yet he turns it down, because the possible ₹50 loss counts for more in his choice.

guided.stem: Before a friendly cricket match, Anjali's captain offers a side bet on a coin toss: win 5 bonus runs or lose 5 runs. Will she likely take it?
guided.hint: Think about how people treat fair bets.

options.text: Probably not; a loss of 5 weighs more.
options.feedback: Right. In choices, losing 5 runs counts for more than gaining 5, so most people turn the bet down.

options.text: Yes, since the bet is fair.
options.feedback: It is fair on paper, but most people still refuse even bets, because the loss counts for more.

options.text: Yes, as gains count for more.
options.feedback: It runs the other way. A loss of one size usually counts for more than the same gain.

steps.takeaway: A loss tends to feel bigger than a gain of the same size.

steps.title: It depends on where you start

hook.stem: Riya hoped for ₹500 from her aunt and got ₹300. Ravi hoped for nothing and got ₹300. Who feels better?

options.text: Ravi.
options.feedback: Right. Ravi got more than he hoped for, so ₹300 feels like a gain.

options.text: Riya.
options.feedback: Riya got less than she hoped for, so ₹300 feels like a loss to her.

options.text: Both feel the same, since both got ₹300.
options.feedback: The money is the same, but each one judges it against a different start.

steps.teach: We judge a result against where we start or what we expect. So the same ₹300 can feel like a gain to one person and a loss to another.

parts: Meghna and Kunal both end the month with ₹1,000, but
Meghna started with ₹1,500,
so her month feels like a loss.
example.spot: Meghna started with ₹1,500,
example.feedback: Her start point was higher than where she ended, so the same ₹1,000 feels like a loss.

guided.stem: One canteen says “Pay ₹5 extra by card.” Another says “Get ₹5 off with cash.” The prices end up the same. What differs?
guided.hint: Work out what you pay at each counter.

options.text: Just the start point in the wording.
options.feedback: Right. The costs match. Only the starting price in the words changes.

options.text: The real cost.
options.feedback: The real cost is the same at both. The wording sets a different start.

options.text: The food on the menu.
options.feedback: The food is not the point. The cost is the same, but the wording sets a different start.

steps.takeaway: Gain or loss depends on where you start.

steps.title: About twice, on average

hook.stem: If a loss weighs more than a gain, by how much, on average?

options.text: About twice as much.
options.feedback: Right. Pooled over many studies, a loss weighed about twice a gain.

options.text: About ten times as much.
options.feedback: That is far too big. The pooled figure was about twice.

options.text: Just a little, about 5% more.
options.feedback: The gap was bigger than that. On average a loss weighed about twice.

steps.teach: Across many studies, a loss weighed about twice a same-size gain, on average. Estimates vary from study to study, so no one person is fixed at exactly two.

visual.label: How much a loss weighs, compared with a gain

example.ask: Tap the part about studies differing.
parts: Pooled over many studies, losses weighed about twice as much,
but the figures differed from study to study,
so the twice is an average.
example.spot: but the figures differed from study to study,
example.feedback: The studies did not all agree, so twice is a middle value, not a rule for everyone.

guided.stem: Kavi says his friend must feel losses exactly twice as much as gains. What is wrong?
guided.hint: Is the figure for a group or for one person?

options.text: Twice is an average; people differ.
options.feedback: Right. The figure is pooled over studies, so one person can be above or below it.

options.text: Losses weigh less than gains.
options.feedback: On average losses weigh more. The point is that twice is an average, not a rule.

options.text: It should be three times.
options.feedback: The pooled figure was about two. The issue is treating an average as a rule.

steps.takeaway: On average a loss weighs about twice a gain; people differ.

concepts.title: Anchoring
concepts.hook: A random number can pull a later estimate: the first figure matters even when it has no link to the answer.
concepts.rule: An early number can pull a later guess toward it, even when it is random. Listing reasons the number might be wrong makes the pull smaller.

claims.text: A first number can pull a later estimate toward it, because people adjust away from it too little.
In one study, a random first number of 10 led to a middle guess of 25, and a random 65 led to a middle guess of 45.
Experienced judges leaned toward a sentence demand even when they set it themselves by rolling dice.
In two studies, listing reasons why an anchor was wrong made its pull smaller.

items.stem: In a school quiz, Ritu is first asked if the Ganga is longer or shorter than 5,000 km, then asked its length. Her friend was first asked about 1,000 km. Who likely guesses a longer length?

options.text: Ritu, who heard the bigger number first.
options.feedback: Each starts from the number in the first question, so the bigger start tends to give the bigger guess.

options.text: Her friend, who heard the smaller number.
options.feedback: A smaller first number tends to pull the guess down, not up.

options.text: Both the same, since the river does not change.
options.feedback: The river is the same, but each guess starts from a different first number.

items.stem: Tejas guessed ₹700 for a bag. He began from a printed tag and came down only a little. So the tag most likely showed ___.

options.text: Far below ₹700, such as ₹200.
options.feedback: He came down from the tag, so it must have been higher than his guess.

options.text: A price of ₹700 itself, the same as his guess.
options.feedback: He moved down a little from the tag, so it was above ₹700, not equal to it.

options.text: A bit above ₹700, such as ₹750.
options.feedback: People adjust too little from the first number, so a small move down points to a tag just above his guess.

items.stem: In one anchor study, people guessing a count of nations who saw a random 10 gave a middle guess of about 25. Those who saw a random 65 gave what middle guess?

options.text: About 45.
options.feedback: The high random number pulled the middle guess up to about 45, short of 65.

options.text: About 65.
options.feedback: People adjusted away from 65, just not far enough, so the guess was lower.

options.text: About 25.
options.feedback: That was the guess after the low number. The high number pulled guesses up.

items.stem: Dr Rao has priced old cars in Mumbai for years. A buyer first mentions a random ₹9 lakh. Will his long experience keep his price free of that number?

options.text: Yes; experts are not swayed by chance numbers.
options.feedback: Studies of judges found expertise and experience did not reduce the pull.

options.text: Yes, as long as the buyer is honest.
options.feedback: Honesty is not the issue. A random first number can pull anyone's guess.

options.text: No; even experts lean toward a random number.
options.feedback: Experienced judges still leaned toward a dice number, so expertise does not switch the pull off.

items.stem: A seller opens at ₹4,000 for a used cricket bat. Which buyer is least pulled by that number?

options.text: Neha, who first lists the bat's dents and worn grip.
options.feedback: Listing reasons the price is too high brings the other side to mind, which shrinks the pull.

options.text: Om, who keeps saying the ₹4,000 to himself.
options.feedback: Repeating the number keeps it in mind, so its pull stays strong.

options.text: Ira, who waits for the seller to name a new price.
options.feedback: Waiting lets the seller set the next number too, so the pull stays.

items.stem: How would you sum up the list-reasons-against-it trick to a friend?

options.text: It removes the anchor's pull for good.
options.feedback: It reduced the pull, but did not remove it, so some pull stays.

options.text: It shrinks the anchor's pull, but some pull stays.
options.feedback: In studies the trick reduced the effect. It did not make the anchor vanish.

options.text: It works by making the first number bigger and easier to see.
options.feedback: The trick does not change the number. It brings reasons against it to mind.

misconceptions.name: First means fair
misconceptions.correction: The first number is a starting point, not proof of the fair value.

misconceptions.name: Random has no pull
misconceptions.correction: Even a number known to be random can sway a later guess.

misconceptions.name: Experts are immune
misconceptions.correction: Experienced judges still leaned toward a random number.

misconceptions.name: One trick erases it
misconceptions.correction: Listing reasons against an anchor shrinks its pull; it does not remove it.

steps.title: A first number pulls your guess

hook.stem: A seller first says a kurta costs ₹2,000, then offers it for ₹1,200. Why does ₹1,200 seem cheap?

options.text: The ₹2,000 came first.
options.feedback: Right. The first price set the starting point, so ₹1,200 looks low next to it.

options.text: ₹1,200 is the usual kurta price.
options.feedback: Nothing here says what kurtas usually cost. The first number shaped the feel.

options.text: The seller is being generous.
options.feedback: The seller set the high first number. That is what makes ₹1,200 seem cheap.

steps.teach: The first number you see becomes a starting point, called an anchor. You adjust away from it, but not far enough, so your guess ends up near it.

parts: Rohit hears “50,000” on TV,
then guesses that 45,000 people fit in the stadium.
example.spot: Rohit hears “50,000” on TV,

guided.stem: Two shops sell the same shoes for ₹1,500. One tag says “was ₹2,500”; the other shows just ₹1,500. Why might the first feel like the better deal?

concepts.title: Confirmation bias
concepts.hook: In Wason's card task, most people turned a card that could prove the rule right and skipped the one that could prove it wrong.
concepts.rule: Confirmation bias is a pull to seek or notice clues that fit a belief. A fair test also looks for clues that could show the belief is wrong.

claims.text: People tend to focus on information that fits what they already believe and pass over what does not.
A rule of the form 'if p then q' is tested properly by checking the cases that could prove it false.
In Wason's number puzzle, only 6 of 29 people found the rule without first naming a wrong one, since cases that fit a guess can fit other rules too.
On the classic card puzzle, only around 1 in 5 people usually pick the cards that could prove the rule wrong.

steps.title: Fitting cases prove little

concepts.title: Social proof
concepts.hook: In Asch's line test, a group giving a plainly wrong answer still pulled some people away from what they could see.
concepts.rule: When we are unsure, a crowd's choice can act as a clue and pull our own. Even when we are sure, a group can pull us to fit in. Group agreement is not proof.

claims.text: In Asch's line test, people went along with a wrong group in 36.8% of answers, against under 1% of mistakes when alone. The group was wrong on 12 of each 18 trials.
When people are unsure, they may follow a group because they believe it has the right information.
A group can agree on a wrong answer, so agreement alone is a clue, not proof.
People differed a lot: about a quarter of Asch's subjects never went along with the wrong group.
In Asch's test the right answer was plain, so people who went along mostly did it to fit in and avoid ridicule; some decided they must be wrong.

options.text: The empty one, since there is no wait for chai.

options.text: Neither; queues put people off.
options.feedback: A queue can put some off, but more often it reads as a sign the stall is good.

options.text: Her friends buying most of the food.
options.feedback: A few friends cannot buy much. The queue is there to be seen, as a sign that others chose it.

options.text: A queue that puts other buyers off.
options.feedback: A queue tends to pull people in, because many others choosing a stall reads as a sign it is good.

concepts.title: The planning fallacy
concepts.hook: In a study, people's guesses for their own tasks ran too short. When they linked past tasks to the new plan, the gap went away.
concepts.rule: The planning fallacy is a tilt toward a short time guess for our own task. Looking at past tasks and missed steps can give a better time guess.

claims.text: People's guesses of how long their own tasks would take were too short, for school tasks and other tasks alike.
In one study, asking people to link past tasks to a new plan removed the too-short bias.
When people plan, they think about how the task will go and pay little heed to how past tasks went.
People guessing how long someone else's task would take guessed long, not short, and used past cases more.
People tended to put their past late finishes down to outside, one-off causes.

misconceptions.correction: Calling each past delay a fluke keeps it out of the next plan, so guesses stay short.

misconceptions.name: Only careless people guess short
misconceptions.correction: Short guesses for our own tasks are common, even for careful planners.

steps.title: We guess too little time

hook.stem: Students guessed when they would finish a big college project. How did their guesses compare with the real time?

options.text: They guessed too little time.
options.feedback: Right. In the studies, people's guesses for their own tasks were too optimistic.

options.text: They were about right.
options.feedback: They were off. People guessed too little time for their own academic and other tasks.

options.text: They guessed too much time.
options.feedback: The other way round. On average, they took longer than they guessed.

steps.teach: Our guesses for our own tasks often run short, at school and outside it. Yet people guessing a friend's task did not guess short, so the slip is about our own plans.

parts: Ishan says his science model will take one evening,
but three evenings later he is still gluing parts.
example.spot: but three evenings later he is still gluing parts.
example.feedback: His guess was far too short. That is the planning fallacy.

guided.stem: Aman plans to clean his hostel room in 20 minutes. It takes an hour. Why is this common?
guided.hint: Think about guesses for our own tasks.

options.text: Most people guess short on their own chores.
options.feedback: Right. Guesses for our own tasks tend to run short.

options.text: Rooms get messier each minute.
options.feedback: The room did not change. His guess was simply too short.

options.text: He was not trying.
options.feedback: Effort is not the issue. Short guesses for our own tasks are common.

steps.takeaway: Your own tasks often take longer than you guess.

steps.title: We picture a smooth path

hook.stem: Kunal plans to print his project in 10 minutes. What might his plan leave out?

options.text: The queue at the print shop.
options.feedback: Right. Plans often picture a smooth path and leave out delays like a queue.

options.text: No step, since printing is quick.
options.feedback: Printing is quick, but getting it done can hit delays, like a queue.

options.text: The colour of the paper.
options.feedback: That will not change the time much. Delays like a queue will.

steps.teach: When we plan, we think through how the task should go and give little thought to how past tasks really went. So delays and extra steps drop out of the guess.

example.ask: Tap the step she left out.
parts: Ritu plans her poster as draw, then colour, but
she forgets the trip to buy chart paper.
example.spot: she forgets the trip to buy chart paper.
example.feedback: The shop trip is a step her smooth plan left out.

guided.stem: Harsh plans to reach the station in 15 minutes. He did not think about traffic. What is his plan missing?
guided.hint: What could slow him on the way?

options.text: Traffic delays.
options.feedback: Yes. A smooth plan often leaves out delays like traffic.

options.text: A faster bike.
options.feedback: The gap in the plan is not the bike. It left out delays.

options.text: No, since 15 minutes is enough.
options.feedback: Maybe on a clear road. His plan did not count delays like traffic.

steps.takeaway: A smooth plan leaves out the delays.

steps.title: Past tasks give a better guess

hook.stem: Your last three lab reports took 2, 3 and 4 hours. A new one is due. What is a fair time guess?

options.text: About 3 hours.
options.feedback: Right. Your past reports are a real guide, and they took about 3 hours.

options.text: About 1 hour, if it goes well.
options.feedback: That pictures a smooth path. Past reports took 2 to 4 hours.

options.text: There is no way to guess.
options.feedback: There is. Past reports took 2 to 4 hours, so about 3 is fair.

steps.teach: How long similar tasks really took is a good guide. We tend to blame past delays on one-off bad luck, so they drop out. In one study, linking past tasks to the new plan removed the short guesses.

nodes: Link them to the new task

so he plans a week again.
example.spot: Yash recalls that his last two speeches took a week to prepare,

guided.stem: A cricket club’s last two match teas took 2 hours to set up. This time they plan 30 minutes. What would give a better guess?
guided.hint: Look at what happened before.

options.text: The 2 hours it took before.
options.feedback: Right. Past setups show the real time, delays and all.

options.text: Hoping it goes faster.
options.feedback: Hope is the smooth plan. Past setups show the real time.

options.text: Asking someone new to guess.
options.feedback: A new guess may also picture a smooth path. Past setups are the better guide.

steps.takeaway: Past tasks show how long the next one may take.

concepts.title: Sleep and memory
concepts.hook: New learning can become more stable during sleep, even without another round of practice.
concepts.rule: Sleep supports the later strengthening and organising of some new memories; it does not replace learning in the first place.

claims.text: Sleep after learning reduced forgetting, compared with the same length of time awake.
A brief spell of quiet rest while awake after learning helped memory more than spending that time on other tasks.
After you learn, a new memory is firmed up over time. This is called consolidation.
In a pilot of 8 people with a mean age of 59, word-pair recall after 12 hours was about 20.4 with sleep and 12.6 awake.
Across 177 papers, people who slept after learning recalled more than people who stayed awake for the same time.

items.stem: A week later, Tanu still recalls a poem easily. Working back, what came first?

options.text: She learned it, then it firmed up over time.
options.feedback: You learn it first, and then the memory firms up over time.

options.text: It firmed up, then she learned it.
options.feedback: A memory has to exist before it can firm up, so learning comes first.

options.text: She heard it once, played aloud while she slept.
options.feedback: Sleep helps store what was learned awake. It does not supply a new poem.

items.stem: In exam week, Yusuf crams new formulas until 3 a.m. and leaves for the exam at 7. What does consolidation suggest?

options.text: Cramming late at night makes new memories firmer by morning.
options.feedback: Late cramming leaves little time and sleep for new memories to firm up.

options.text: His new formulas have had little time to firm up.
options.feedback: Firming up takes time after learning, and he left very little of it.

options.text: Firming up is done the moment he reads.
options.feedback: The memory firms up over time after you learn, not at the very moment you read.

items.stem: In a small sleep pilot, recall after sleep was about 60% higher than after the same hours awake. If that gap held in a chemistry class and the awake group recalled 10 new terms, about how many might the sleepers recall?

options.text: About 16 terms.
options.feedback: Right. 60% more than 10 is 6 more, so about 16, if the pilot's gap held for chemistry terms.

options.text: About 10 terms.
options.feedback: That leaves out the gap. In the pilot, sleepers recalled about 60% more than people who stayed awake.

options.text: About 70 terms.
options.feedback: That adds 60 terms, not 60%. Six tenths of 10 is 6, so about 16 terms.

items.stem: Before a college viva, Imran thinks sleep is wasted time and stays up to keep his notes fresh. What does the research suggest?

options.text: Staying awake keeps new memories fresher.
options.feedback: Studies found more forgetting after time awake than after sleep.

options.text: Sleep after study tends to cut forgetting.
options.feedback: Sleep after study cut forgetting, compared with the same hours spent awake.

options.text: Sleep just pauses the brain for the night.
options.feedback: The sleeping brain helps firm up new memories, so it is not a mere pause.

items.stem: Match each case to what it does for memory.

options.text: A night of sleep after study
options.feedback: Sleep after you learn cuts down on how much you forget.

options.text: Less forgetting the next day
options.feedback: This is what sleep after learning tends to give.

options.text: Ten quiet minutes, eyes shut
options.feedback: Quiet rest after learning helped memory more than busy tasks.

options.text: Can help a new memory settle
options.feedback: This matches a short spell of quiet rest after learning.

options.text: Skipping the lesson itself
options.feedback: With no learning, there is no new memory at all.

options.text: Nothing to firm up later
options.feedback: Consolidation needs a memory to work on, so a skipped lesson gives none.

items.stem: How would you describe a study break that helps memory to a friend?

options.text: Jump straight into reels for a while to relax the mind.
options.feedback: Reels are a busy task. Quiet rest with nothing to do is what helped.

options.text: Breaks undo what you just learned.
options.feedback: Quiet breaks after learning helped memory in studies, so they do not undo it.

options.text: Rest quietly a few minutes before the next task.
options.feedback: Quiet rest after learning helped memory more than jumping into other tasks.

misconceptions.name: Sleep is only a pause
misconceptions.correction: The brain can process recent learning during sleep.

misconceptions.name: Sleep teaches unseen material
misconceptions.correction: Sleep can help store what was learned, but it does not supply an unread lesson.

steps.title: Learn first, then it firms up

hook.stem: Rohan sleeps with his textbook under his pillow but never opens it. Will he remember the chapter?

options.text: No, he never learned it.
options.feedback: Right. Sleep can firm up a memory, but only one he has already learned.

options.text: Yes, sleep will add it.
options.feedback: Sleep helps store what was learned. It cannot add a chapter he never read.

options.text: Yes, if he sleeps long enough.
options.feedback: No amount of sleep can store a chapter he never opened.

steps.teach: You learn first, and then the new memory firms up over time. That later step is called consolidation, so sleep cannot store a lesson you never took in.

parts: Divya reads her notes on the Mughals carefully,
and a week later the dates still come back easily.
example.spot: Divya reads her notes on the Mughals carefully,
example.feedback: Reading carefully is the learning step. Only after it can the memory firm up and last.

guided.stem: Faisal learns ten new Hindi words today. Over the next days the words feel steadier. What is that later step called?
guided.hint: It is the firming up after learning.

options.text: Consolidation.
options.feedback: Yes. Consolidation is the firming up of a memory after learning.

options.text: Learning.
options.feedback: Learning came first, today. The later firming up is consolidation.

options.text: Forgetting.
options.feedback: The words are getting steadier, not fading. That is consolidation.

steps.takeaway: Learn first; the memory firms up later.

steps.title: Sleep helps memories last

hook.stem: Two groups learn word pairs. One sleeps, the other stays awake for the same hours. Which group recalls more later?

options.text: The group that slept.
options.feedback: Right. In many studies, sleep after learning helps later recall.

options.text: The group that stayed awake.
options.feedback: Staying awake did not help more. In studies, sleep after learning helped recall.

options.text: Both recall the same.
options.feedback: In many studies, the sleep group recalled more.

steps.teach: Sleep after learning cuts forgetting compared with the same hours awake, since the sleeping brain helps firm up new memories. A big review found a moderate gain for facts and words.

example.ask: Tap what came between learning and morning.
parts: Gautam learns the names of ten ragas in the evening,
sleeps,
and the next morning he still recalls most of them.
example.spot: sleeps,
example.feedback: Sleep after learning can cut how much of new facts and names is forgotten.

guided.stem: Sara learns a list of capitals at night, then sleeps. Ali learns it in the morning and stays awake all day. Who may recall more after the same gap?
guided.hint: Who slept after learning?

options.text: Sara.
options.feedback: Yes. Sleep after learning can help later recall.

options.text: Ali.
options.feedback: Ali stayed awake. In studies, sleep after learning tended to help recall more.

options.text: Neither can recall anything.
options.feedback: Both can recall some. Sleep after learning can help Sara recall more.

steps.takeaway: Sleep after learning helps new memories stick.

steps.title: Quiet rest helps too

hook.stem: After a lesson, Jaya sits quietly for ten minutes with her eyes closed. Can that help her memory?

options.text: Yes, quiet rest can help.
options.feedback: Right. A short spell of quiet rest after learning helped memory in studies.

options.text: No, sleep is the one thing that helps.
options.feedback: Sleep helps, but quiet rest while awake helped memory too.

options.text: No, it is a waste of time.
options.feedback: Studies found that quiet rest after learning helped memory.

steps.teach: Sleep is not the only help. A few minutes of quiet rest after learning, awake with nothing to do, helped memory more than doing other tasks, so a calm break can count.

parts: After learning a list of new biology terms,
Lakshmi sits quietly for a few minutes,
and later she recalls the terms well.
example.spot: Lakshmi sits quietly for a few minutes,
example.feedback: Quiet rest after learning can help new memories firm up.

guided.stem: Between two exams, Rhea naps for a bit, then rests with her eyes closed. Which can help her new memories?
guided.hint: Can a wakeful break help as well?

options.text: Both the nap and the quiet rest.
options.feedback: Yes. Sleep can help, and quiet waking rest can help too.

options.text: Just the nap.
options.feedback: The nap can help, and so can quiet waking rest.

options.text: Neither.
options.feedback: Both can help new memories firm up.

steps.takeaway: Sleep helps memory, and so can quiet rest while awake.

concepts.title: Variable rewards
concepts.hook: A surprise good post can make the next swipe tempting, even after several dull ones.
concepts.rule: When rewards arrive after an unknown number of tries, the next try can seem worth making. This helps explain repeated checking, though apps and people have other reasons too.

claims.text: On a variable schedule, people keep responding at a high, steady rate because they never know when the next reward is coming, and the habit is slow to fade.
Apps use several features besides surprise rewards, such as endless scrolling and read ticks that turn blue, which can stretch the time people spend on them.
On a variable schedule, the number of tries needed for a reward keeps changing, so you cannot tell which try will bring it.
A reward after every try is the quickest way to teach a new behaviour.
In over a million posts, people spaced their posts in a way that collected more likes, and people use social media for many motives.

items.stem: Which of these is a variable reward?

options.text: A lucky draw on UPI payments, won at random.
options.feedback: You cannot tell which payment will win, so the reward is variable.

options.text: Cashback of ₹10 on every fifth payment you make.
options.feedback: Every fifth payment is a set count, so you know when it comes. That is fixed.

options.text: A ₹5 discount on each payment.
options.feedback: A reward on each payment comes every time, so there is nothing to guess.

items.stem: Saina is teaching her younger brother to put his shoes on the rack. Why might she praise him each time at first, not now and then?

options.text: Uneven, now-and-then praise teaches a brand new act fastest.
options.feedback: Uneven rewards keep an act going. For teaching it first, a reward each time is quicker.

options.text: A reward on each try teaches a new act fastest.
options.feedback: Rewarding every time is the quickest way to teach a new behaviour, so it suits the start.

options.text: Praise has no effect on new acts.
options.feedback: Rewards do shape new acts. Rewarding every time teaches fastest.

items.stem: In a feed with variable rewards, each swipe has a 1-in-5 chance of a fun clip. After five swipes, what is the chance of at least one?

options.text: About 67%.
options.feedback: The chance of no clip five times is 0.8 to the fifth, about 33%, so at least one is about 67%.

options.text: 100%, since one in five means a clip by swipe five.
options.feedback: Chances do not stack that neatly. Five misses in a row can still happen.

options.text: 20%, the same as one swipe.
options.feedback: More swipes give more chances, so the total rises above one swipe's chance.

items.stem: At the train station, one machine gives a cup of chai each time a coin goes in. A lucky-draw box pays now and then. Both stop paying. Where will people keep trying longer?

options.text: At the chai machine, since it paid each time before.
options.feedback: When a reward that came each time stops, people notice fast and give up sooner.

options.text: At the lucky-draw box.
options.feedback: When rewards come at unknown times, a pause looks normal, so people keep trying there longer.

options.text: Both the same, since both stopped.
options.feedback: Both stopped, but uneven rewards fade much more slowly than steady ones.

items.stem: Zoya, a college student, turns off all like alerts, yet she still opens her chat app many times a day. Working back, what does that suggest?

options.text: Other pulls, like news from friends, keep her opening it.
options.feedback: Right. Surprise likes are one pull, but people also open apps for friends and news, so many things keep them coming back.

options.text: Her alerts must still be on.
options.feedback: She turned them off. Opening the app anyway points to other pulls, such as wanting news from friends.

options.text: Surprise likes are the one reason people open apps.
options.feedback: If likes were the whole story, turning off alerts would end it. Friends, news and design also pull people back.

items.stem: Arjun says feeds are slot machines and no other thing keeps people scrolling. What is not quite right?

options.text: Surprise rewards are one pull among several.
options.feedback: Apps also use endless scroll and read ticks, and people come for friends and news.

options.text: Feeds pay out on a fixed count.
options.feedback: Feeds do not pay on a set count. The point is that rewards are only one pull.

options.text: Slot machines share no features with feeds.
options.feedback: They share uneven rewards. But feeds also use other hooks.

misconceptions.name: Every swipe rewards
misconceptions.correction: A good result can come after dull ones, with no set gap.

misconceptions.name: One cause explains all use
misconceptions.correction: People open feeds for many reasons, and apps use several hooks, not just uncertain rewards.

misconceptions.name: It is just weak will
misconceptions.correction: Rewards that come at unknown times keep checks going for most people, not only the weak-willed.

steps.title: Variable means you cannot tell when

hook.stem: A game gives a prize after some rounds but not others, with no pattern. How would you describe these prizes?

options.text: They come at uneven times.
options.feedback: Right. When a reward comes at uneven, unknown times, it is called variable.

options.text: They come after every round.
options.feedback: Not every round pays. Some do and some do not, with no pattern.

options.text: They come every fifth round.
options.feedback: That would be a fixed pattern. Here the prize comes at uneven times.

steps.teach: With a variable reward, the number of tries before a prize keeps changing, so you cannot tell which try will pay. A reward on every try is different: it teaches a new act fastest.

parts: Each time Zubin opens his messages,
there might be a reply or nothing at all.
example.spot: there might be a reply or nothing at all.
example.feedback: Sometimes a reply, sometimes nothing, with no way to tell. That is a variable reward.

options.text: No, it is fixed.
options.feedback: Right. You know the star comes every third time, so it is fixed.

options.text: Yes, stars are variable.
options.feedback: Here the star always comes every third time. That is fixed.

options.text: Yes, because it is a reward.
options.feedback: Any reward can be fixed or variable. This one comes on a set count.

steps.title: Not knowing keeps you checking

hook.stem: A scratch-card game pays out on some cards but not others, with no pattern. Why do people keep buying cards?

options.text: The next card might win.
options.feedback: Right. No one can tell which card will pay, so each new one seems worth a try.

options.text: Each card wins something.
options.feedback: Most cards win nothing. The pull is that the next one might.

options.text: The seller makes them buy.
options.feedback: Nobody forces them. Not knowing which card pays keeps people buying.

steps.teach: When the next try might pay, it seems worth making, so people keep going. Gambling runs on this kind of reward, which is why such habits are slow to fade.

parts: Nikita finds a funny meme only now and then,
so she keeps swiping in case the next one is good.
example.spot: so she keeps swiping in case the next one is good.
example.feedback: Not knowing when the next good one comes keeps her swiping.

guided.stem: In a cricket card game, rare cards turn up in random packs. Omkar keeps opening packs. Why?
guided.hint: Can he tell which pack has a rare card?

options.text: The next one could be the lucky one.
options.feedback: Yes. He cannot tell which pack has a rare card, so each new one is worth a try.

options.text: Every pack has a rare card.
options.feedback: Rare cards turn up in random packs, not in every one.

options.text: He has to open every pack.
options.feedback: Nothing forces him. Not knowing which pack pays keeps him going.

steps.takeaway: Not knowing when a reward comes keeps us trying.

steps.title: One pull, not the whole story

hook.stem: Mansi opens a chat app many times a day. What could be the reason?

options.text: Many reasons, like friends, news or a break.
options.feedback: Right. People open apps for many reasons, and surprise rewards are just one.

options.text: Just the hope of a surprise reward.
options.feedback: Surprise rewards are one pull, but people have other reasons too.

options.text: Because the app is new.
options.feedback: Newness is not the main reason. People open apps for friends, news and more.

steps.teach: Surprise rewards are one pull, not the whole story. Apps also use endless scroll and read ticks that turn blue, and people open them for friends or news, so many things keep us on.

parts: Kiran opens his feed after class
to see what his cousins posted from the wedding.
example.spot: to see what his cousins posted from the wedding.
example.feedback: His reason is family news, not a surprise reward. People open feeds for many reasons.

guided.stem: Tanmay keeps opening a cricket score app during a match. What is the most likely reason?
guided.hint: What does a score app give him?

options.text: He wants to know who is winning.
options.feedback: Right. A score app gives him the latest news on the match.

options.text: Just the hope of a surprise prize.
options.feedback: Surprise rewards are one pull, but here he simply wants the latest score.

options.text: The app forces him.
options.feedback: Nothing forces him. He opens it to keep up with the match.

steps.takeaway: Uneven rewards are one pull, not the whole story.

concepts.title: If-then plans
concepts.hook: A plan tied to a clear moment can help turn a goal into an action.
concepts.rule: An if-then plan names a cue and the action to take when it appears. This link can help people start.

claims.text: An if-then plan spells out the when, where and how in advance: if situation Y comes, then I will do X.
Across 94 tests, if-then plans had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals, on average.
If-then plans make the named moment easier to spot and the response to it more automatic.
When a plan worked by sharpening the cue, other cues were more often passed over.
A 2025 review of 642 tests found if-then plans helped thinking, feelings and actions, with effects from small to medium-large.

items.stem: Rohit wants to call home more from his hostel. Which if-then plan fits best?

options.text: I will call home more often from now on.
options.feedback: This is a goal with no moment named, so nothing tells him when to call.

options.text: If I finish Sunday lunch, then I call my parents.
options.feedback: It names a clear moment and one action, which is what an if-then plan needs.

options.text: If I miss home, then I will think about it.
options.feedback: Missing home is a vague moment, and thinking is not a clear action.

items.stem: Tanya's diary says: every time the 6 p.m. temple bell rings, she waters the plants. Turned into an if-then line, the if part is ___.

options.text: Watering the plants.
options.feedback: Watering is the action, so it belongs in the then part.

options.text: Wanting a green balcony.
options.feedback: That is the goal behind it. The if part is the moment, the bell.

options.text: The bell ringing at 6.
options.feedback: The bell is the moment that starts the act, so it goes in the if part.

items.stem: Isha's plan: “If the 8 p.m. hostel bell rings, then I revise.” One evening her room is free and quiet at 6, long before the bell. What might the plan make her do?

options.text: Notice every free hour just as well as she notices the bell.
options.feedback: Plans that sharpen one cue tended to make other cues easier to pass over.

options.text: Pass over the quiet hour and wait for the bell.
options.feedback: A sharp cue can make other good chances easier to miss, so she may wait for the bell.

options.text: Revise for twice as long that night.
options.feedback: Nothing in the plan doubles the time. The risk is missing the earlier chance.

items.stem: Why does “If I board the metro, then I open my flashcards” work better than “I will revise on the way”?

options.text: Metro rides are longer than other rides.
options.feedback: Ride length is not the point. The plan names a clear moment and act.

options.text: Saying the word if makes the brain promise to act on time.
options.feedback: Plans help on average but promise nothing. The clear cue is what helps.

options.text: It names a moment you will spot and the act to start.
options.feedback: It links a clear cue to one action, and a clear cue is easy to notice.

items.stem: In an older review of 94 tests of if-then plans, effects are scored where 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. About what was the average effect?

options.text: About 0.65.
options.feedback: The average effect was about 0.65, between medium and large.

options.text: About 0.1.
options.feedback: That would be tiny. The pooled effect was medium to large.

options.text: About 2.5.
options.feedback: That is far above large on this scale. The average was about 0.65.

items.stem: A coaching ad claims one if-then plan will make any student top the class. What is too strong?

options.text: If-then plans have no effect on how students do in the end.
options.feedback: They did have an effect, medium to large on average.

options.text: Plans help on average; they cannot promise results.
options.feedback: Across many tests the plans helped on average, which is not a promise for each student.

options.text: The plan works for top students alone.
options.feedback: Nothing limits it to top students. The issue is the promise of a result.

misconceptions.correction: A broad goal leaves the moment of action unnamed.

misconceptions.name: A plan guarantees action
misconceptions.correction: If-then plans help on average, but a cue can still be missed.

misconceptions.name: A sharp cue has no cost
misconceptions.correction: Focusing on one named cue can make other good chances easier to miss.

steps.title: Link a moment to an action

hook.stem: Three students plan to revise. Who has a clear moment to start?

options.text: Asha: “If I finish dinner, then I open my notes.”
options.feedback: Right. Her plan links a clear moment, dinner ending, to one action.

options.text: Bunty: “I will revise more this week.”
options.feedback: That is a goal, but it names no moment to start.

options.text: Chirag: “I hope to revise sometime.”
options.feedback: A hope names no moment or action. An if-then plan names both.

steps.teach: An if-then plan links a moment to an action: “If this happens, then I will do that.” The moment is the cue to start, so the plan names when and what.

parts: Ananya decides that
when the school bell rings at 4,
she will walk to the library.
example.spot: when the school bell rings at 4,
example.feedback: The bell is the if part: the clear moment that starts the action.

guided.stem: Tara’s plan: “If I tie my shoes after school, then I go for a run.” Which part is the action?
guided.hint: The action is the then part.

options.text: Going for a run.
options.feedback: Right. The then part names the action.

options.text: Tying her shoes.
options.feedback: That is the if part, the cue.

options.text: Getting out of school.
options.feedback: That is when the cue happens. The action is the run.

steps.takeaway: If this moment comes, then I do that action.

steps.title: Pick a moment you will notice

hook.stem: Which cue is easiest to notice: “when I feel like it,” “when I have time,” or “when the 7 o’clock news ends”?

options.text: When the 7 o’clock news ends.
options.feedback: Right. It is a clear moment you cannot miss.

options.text: When I feel like it.
options.feedback: That feeling may never come at a clear moment.

options.text: When I have time.
options.feedback: Free time is hard to spot, so it may not start the action.

steps.teach: A clear moment, like “after dinner,” stays on your mind, so you spot it when it comes. A vague goal names no moment. One catch: you may pass over other good chances.

parts: Instead of planning to practise someday, Dhruv picks a moment:
when he gets home from school,
he plays the flute.
example.spot: when he gets home from school,
example.feedback: Getting home is a clear moment, so it is easy to notice.

guided.stem: Sonal says, “I will drink more water.” Which line turns it into an if-then plan?
guided.hint: Look for a clear moment and an action.

options.text: “If I sit down for lunch, then I drink a glass of water.”
options.feedback: Yes. It links a clear moment to one action.

options.text: “I really want to drink more water.”
options.feedback: That is still a wish, with no moment to start.

options.text: “I will try hard.”
options.feedback: Trying hard names no moment. An if-then plan needs a cue.

steps.takeaway: A clear moment is easy to notice; a vague one is easy to miss.

steps.title: It helps, but cannot promise

hook.stem: Studies compared people with only a goal to people who also made an if-then plan. What did they find?

options.text: The plans helped on average.
options.feedback: Right. Across 94 tests, people with if-then plans reached goals more often.

options.text: The plans made no difference.
options.feedback: They did make a difference: a medium-to-large effect on average.

options.text: Everyone with a plan acted every time.
options.feedback: Plans helped on average, but not every person acted every time.

steps.teach: In an older review of 94 tests, people with if-then plans reached goals more often than those with a goal alone. A 2025 review of 642 tests agreed, so plans help but cannot promise action.

visual.label: How much if-then plans helped, in an older review of 94 tests

example.ask: Tap where the plan did not work.
parts: Govind plans, “If I wake up, then I stretch,” and he stretches most days,
but not on the day he oversleeps.
example.spot: but not on the day he oversleeps.
example.feedback: The plan helps on most days, but it cannot promise every time.

guided.stem: Two cricket teams set a goal to practise catching. One team also adds if-then plans. Which team is likely to practise more?
guided.hint: What did studies find on average?

options.text: The team with if-then plans.
options.feedback: Right. On average, if-then plans helped people act on goals.

options.text: The team with just the goal.
options.feedback: Studies found the opposite, on average.

options.text: No difference.
options.feedback: Across 94 tests, plans made a real difference on average.

steps.takeaway: If-then plans help on average, but they cannot promise action.

concepts.title: The spotlight effect
concepts.hook: A small slip can feel huge to us. Others may notice it less.
concepts.rule: The spotlight effect means we guess that more people notice us than really do. Some still notice, and they tend to judge our slips more kindly than we fear.

claims.text: In two studies, people wearing a T-shirt with a striking image guessed that more people could recall it than really could.
In a group talk, speakers thought their good and bad remarks stood out more to others than they did.
After a public slip, people expected others to judge them more harshly than others really did.
People seem to start from their own rich view of a moment and adjust too little for how others see it.
The fear of harsh judgment came partly from people dwelling on their own mishap and forgetting what else onlookers take into account.

items.stem: Before a college viva, Sanjana gets a pimple on her nose and worries the panel will remember it. What is most likely?

options.text: Each panel member will recall it clearly.
options.feedback: That is the spotlight guess. Others notice and recall far less than we expect.

options.text: The panel will mark her down for it.
options.feedback: A viva is marked on answers. And few will even recall the pimple.

options.text: Few on the panel will recall it later.
options.feedback: People tend to overrate how much others notice them, so the panel will likely recall little.

items.stem: Made-up numbers: Arnav guessed 12 classmates would recall the picture on his bright shirt. His guess was 7 too high. How many could really recall it?

options.text: About 5.
options.feedback: If 12 was 7 too high, the real count is 12 minus 7, which is 5.

options.text: About 19.
options.feedback: That adds the 7 on. His guess was too high, so the real count is lower.

options.text: About 12.
options.feedback: That is his guess. The real count was 7 lower than that.

items.stem: In an online college class, Varsha's video freezes on a funny face for a few seconds. Because it felt huge to her, she says the whole class must have noticed. What is not quite right?

options.text: It felt huge because she lived it in full detail.
options.feedback: Right. She saw every second from the inside. Classmates caught a brief moment, so far fewer noticed than she thinks.

options.text: No slip; a big feeling means many noticed.
options.feedback: How big a moment feels to us says little about others. We live our own moments in close-up.

options.text: Online classes hide frozen screens from view.
options.feedback: Some classmates may have seen it. The slip is guessing that all of them did, because it felt so big.

items.stem: Kiran makes a clever point in a group talk and thinks everyone will remember it. Does the spotlight effect apply here?

options.text: No; it covers embarrassing slips alone.
options.feedback: It is not limited to slips. Good remarks were also overrated.

options.text: Yes; we overrate how much good moments stand out too.
options.feedback: In the study, speakers overrated how much both good and bad remarks stood out.

options.text: No; clever points get remembered by everyone in the room later.
options.feedback: Others noticed both good and bad remarks less than speakers thought.

items.stem: Which line sums up what the slip studies found?

options.text: People were judged more harshly than they feared.
options.feedback: It went the other way. The fear was bigger than the real judgment.

options.text: Onlookers judged the slips without any thought.
options.feedback: Onlookers did think. They weighed the whole situation, which softened their view.

options.text: People feared harsher judgment than they got.
options.feedback: Across four studies, people expected to be judged more harshly than they were.

items.stem: Yash drops his tray on the wet canteen floor. He replays it all night and fears everyone thinks he is clumsy. Both errors come from ___.

options.text: living the slip up close and missing the wet floor
options.feedback: Right. Seen from the inside, the slip looms large, and fixing on it hides the wet floor that onlookers saw.

options.text: other students staring at him all night
options.feedback: Onlookers glance and move on. The night of replays comes from his own close-up view of the slip.

options.text: how heavy the tray was
options.feedback: The tray's weight explains nothing about his fears. He lived the slip up close and forgot the wet floor.

misconceptions.name: Everyone noticed
misconceptions.correction: Our own vivid view can make an event seem more visible to others than it was.

misconceptions.name: Nobody ever notices
misconceptions.correction: Some people may take note. The guess is often too high.

misconceptions.name: Others judge us harshly
misconceptions.correction: After a slip, people judged us more kindly than we expected.

misconceptions.name: Only embarrassing moments
misconceptions.correction: We also overrate how much our good moments stand out to others.

steps.title: Fewer people notice than we think

hook.stem: Sumit spills chai on his shirt before class. He thinks the whole class sees it. What is more likely?

options.text: Fewer people notice than he thinks.
options.feedback: Right. In a study, people guessed twice as many noticed their shirt as really did.

options.text: Everyone notices.
options.feedback: In studies, far fewer noticed than people guessed.

options.text: No one notices.
options.feedback: Some may notice, just fewer than he thinks.

steps.teach: We tend to think more people notice us than really do. In one study, people in an odd T-shirt guessed too high how many others could recall it, so the spotlight felt brighter than it was.

parts: Prerna gets a bad haircut and hides all day, yet
at lunch only one friend says anything.
example.spot: at lunch only one friend says anything.
example.feedback: Far fewer people noticed than she feared.

guided.stem: On a train, Ayesha’s phone rings loudly with a funny ringtone. She thinks the whole coach will remember. What is going on?
guided.hint: Compare her guess with what others notice.

options.text: She guesses more noticed than really did.
options.feedback: Right. That gap between her guess and what others notice is the spotlight effect.

options.text: Everyone really will remember.
options.feedback: Fewer people notice and recall than we tend to think.

options.text: No one could hear it.
options.feedback: Some may hear it. The point is she guesses too many will remember.

steps.takeaway: Fewer people notice us than we think.

steps.title: Our own view makes it loom large

hook.stem: Why does a small slip in a speech feel so big to the speaker?

options.text: They felt every second of it.
options.feedback: Right. The speaker lives every detail, so the slip looms large to them.

options.text: The crowd talks about it for days.
options.feedback: Most listeners notice far less. It feels big because the speaker lived it.

options.text: Slips are big by nature.
options.feedback: A small slip is small to others. It feels big from the inside.

steps.teach: We live every detail of our own moments, good or bad, so they feel huge to us. We start from that vivid view and do not adjust enough for how little others saw.

example.ask: Tap how big it felt to him.
parts: Arush says one wrong word in his group talk,
and he replays it all night,
though no one mentions it.
example.spot: and he replays it all night,
example.feedback: His own vivid view makes the slip loom larger for him than for the others.

guided.stem: Mohan drops an easy catch in a friendly match and thinks the whole team will talk about it. What is going on?
guided.hint: Compare how it feels to him and to others.

options.text: To him it looms larger than to them.
options.feedback: Yes. He lived the drop in full detail; his teammates saw one quick moment.

options.text: The team will talk about it for a week.
options.feedback: Others notice our slips far less than we think, so a week of talk is unlikely.

options.text: He did not really drop it.
options.feedback: He did drop it. The point is that it feels bigger to him than to them.

steps.takeaway: A slip feels bigger to you than to others.

steps.title: Others judge us more kindly

hook.stem: You give a wrong answer out loud in class. How harshly will classmates judge you, compared with your fear?

options.text: Less harshly than you fear.
options.feedback: Right. In studies, people expected harsher judgment than they really got.

options.text: Just as harshly as you fear.
options.feedback: In studies, the fear ran ahead of what others really thought.

options.text: Far more harshly than you fear.
options.feedback: It went the other way. Others judged slips more kindly than people feared.

steps.teach: After a slip, people expected others to judge them more harshly than others really did. We dwell on the slip itself, so we forget that onlookers weigh the whole situation.

parts: Nikhil trips while carrying the trophy,
and he fears the hall thinks he is clumsy,
but most just notice the stage is slippery.
example.spot: but most just notice the stage is slippery.
example.feedback: Onlookers take in the whole scene, like a slippery stage, so they judge him more kindly.

guided.stem: Why might onlookers go easy on someone who flubs a hard quiz question?
guided.hint: What do onlookers see that the speaker forgets?

options.text: They see how hard the question was.
options.feedback: Yes. Onlookers weigh the whole situation, such as a tough question.

options.text: They did not hear the question.
options.feedback: They heard it. They also see how tough it was, which softens their view.

options.text: They have short memories.
options.feedback: Memory is not the reason. They take the hard question into account.

steps.takeaway: Others usually judge our slips more kindly than we fear.
